content: Alcacuz, also known as Chinese licorice or gan cao, is used for various medical conditions, with specific dosing recommendations. The powdered root is typically administered orally in doses of 5 to 1 gram, taken once to three times daily (qD-TID). It is advised not to use this treatment for more than 4 to 6 weeks. Indications: This herbal remedy is utilized for conditions such as adrenocortical insufficiency, arthritis, bronchitis, dry cough, peptic ulcers, gastritis, bacterial and viral infections, prostate cancer, sore throat, systemic lupus erythematosus, and upper respiratory inflammation. Drug Interactions: Licorice can enhance the effects of digoxin through pharmacodynamic synergism. However, the clinical significance of this interaction is considered minor or unknown. Adverse Effects: Reported adverse effects include amenorrhea, congestive heart failure (CHF), decreased libido, edema, erectile dysfunction, headache, hypertension, hypertensive encephalopathy, hypokalemia, hypokalemic myopathy, lethargy, lower extremity weakness, mineralocorticoid effects, myoglobinuria, pulmonary edema, quadriplegia, rhabdomyolysis, sodium and fluid retention, and systemic effects related to electrolyte imbalances. Contraindications: Licorice is contraindicated in individuals with breast cancer, cholestatic liver disorders, cirrhosis, CHF, diabetes mellitus, endometriosis, hormone-sensitive conditions, hypertonia, hypersensitivity to licorice, hypertension, hypokalemia, ovarian cancer, severe renal insufficiency, uterine cancer, and uterine fibroids. It should also be avoided in patients taking CYP3A4 substrates or potassium-depleting agents, as well as those with impaired liver function. FDA Consumer Alert: The FDA has issued a warning that consuming more than 2 ounces of licorice per day for at least 2 weeks may lead to hypokalemia and arrhythmias. Adults aged 40 or older are at a higher risk of these complications (October 2011). Pregnancy and Lactation: Licorice is considered unsafe during pregnancy and should be avoided during lactation. While some substances are generally acceptable during pregnancy (Category A), licorice does not fall into this category due to potential risks. Pharmacological Properties: Licorice exhibits anti-inflammatory and expectorant properties. It works by blocking the metabolism of prostaglandins PGE2 and PGF2-alpha. However, deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) is less effective for upper respiratory conditions. Metabolism and Excretion: Specific details regarding the metabolism and excretion of licorice are not available (N/A). This information highlights the therapeutic uses, risks, and limitations of licorice, emphasizing the importance of cautious use under medical supervision.
